name: Database Concepts, File Systems & Data Models

questions.question: Match each basic file-system term to its definition.

pairs.right: Raw facts, with little meaning until organized
A character or group of characters with a specific meaning
A logically connected set of fields describing one person, place or thing
A collection of related records, in a non-DBMS system
A collection of related records, inside a DBMS

questions.explanation: File and Table have the same definition — the name changes depending on whether you're in a file-based system or a DBMS.

questions.question: Each file-system term has a database equivalent. Match them.

pairs.right: Attribute
Entity instance
Entity

questions.explanation: Field = attribute, record = entity instance, table = entity. These pairs come up constantly once you start drawing ERDs.

questions.question: "Raw facts, such as a telephone number or a birth date, that have little meaning unless organized in some logical manner" is the definition of:
questions.explanation: That's data. Information is what you get after data is processed and given context.

questions.question: A character or group of characters, alpha or numeric, that has a specific meaning is called a ______.
questions.explanation: A field — known as an attribute once you're talking in database terms.

questions.question: In a DBMS, a collection of related records is called a table. In a file-based system, the same collection is called a:
questions.explanation: Same definition, different name: file outside a DBMS, table inside one.

questions.question: Databases can be classified by the degree of structure in their data. Match each level to its description.

pairs.right: Data exists in its original, raw state
Data results from formatting, applied to suit a type of processing
Data that has been partially processed — XML, for instance

questions.explanation: XML is the standard example of semistructured data: it represents data elements in a textual format without imposing a full relational structure.

questions.question: XML — the usual example of semistructured data — stands for Extensible ______ Language.
questions.explanation: Extensible Markup Language. It represents data elements in a textual format.

questions.question: Databases can also be classified by location. Match each type to its description.

pairs.right: Data is located at a single site
Data is spread across several different sites
Created and maintained with cloud services that provide defined performance measures

questions.explanation: Location-based classification: one site, many sites, or a cloud provider's infrastructure.

questions.question: A database that stores historical data and business metrics used exclusively for tactical or strategic decision making is a(n):
questions.explanation: Analytical databases support decision making. Transactional (operational) databases support day-to-day operations.

questions.question: Match each decision-support term to what it actually is.

pairs.right: Stores data in a format optimized for decision support
Tools that retrieve, process and model data from a data warehouse
Capturing and processing business data to generate information supporting decisions

questions.explanation: OLAP stands for online analytical processing — the tooling layer that sits over the warehouse.

questions.question: OLAP stands for online ______ processing.
questions.explanation: Online analytical processing — the tools used to retrieve, process and model data from a data warehouse.

questions.question: Modern end-user productivity tools such as Microsoft Excel are a kind of "file system redux" — they reintroduce file-system problems.
questions.explanation: Spreadsheets are a file system redux: convenient, but they bring back redundancy and inconsistency.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a problem of file systems?
options: Difficulty getting quick answers to ad hoc queries
questions.explanation: File systems don't enforce referential integrity at all — that's one of the things a DBMS adds.

questions.question: Match each dependence/independence term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Access to a file depends on its own structure, so programs must change when the structure does
The file structure can change without affecting the application's ability to access the data
Data access changes when data storage characteristics change
Storage characteristics can change without affecting the program's ability to access data

questions.explanation: Structural is about the shape of the file; data is about how it's physically stored. In both cases, independence is the goal.

questions.question: The practical significance of data dependence is the difference between the logical and physical format. Which describes the LOGICAL format?
options: How the data is actually stored on the hardware
How the data is represented to the application or user
The order blocks are written to disk
The compression algorithm applied to the file
questions.explanation: Logical = the representation to the application or user. Physical = actual storage on hardware, which should be hidden completely and of no concern to the user.

questions.question: The physical format — how data is actually stored on hardware — should be hidden completely from the end user.
questions.explanation: Physical storage should be hidden completely and of no concern to the user.

questions.question: Compared with a file system, a database system provides:
options: Less data independence, but faster raw file access
More data independence, more robust organization, and better control of data access
Identical data independence, with only a different user interface
questions.explanation: The three advantages are exactly these: more data independence, more robust organization, better control of data access.

questions.question: Unnecessarily storing the same data at different places is called data ______.
questions.explanation: Data redundancy. It creates "islands of information" and raises the odds of different versions of the same data existing at once.

questions.question: Scattered, duplicated data locations are described with the phrase:
questions.explanation: Islands of information — the same data kept in several disconnected places.

questions.question: Which is NOT listed as a possible result of uncontrolled data redundancy?
questions.explanation: Poor security, inconsistency, data-entry errors, integrity problems and anomalies are the listed consequences. Performance is not among them.

questions.question: Anomalies develop when not all of the required changes in redundant data are made ______.
questions.explanation: If redundant copies are only partly updated, the data disagrees with itself — that's an anomaly.

questions.question: Match each anomaly to what goes wrong.

pairs.right: Changed data ends up inconsistent or incomplete
New data cannot be recorded completely
Removing one fact partially removes another

questions.explanation: These three are the reason normalization exists — they all come from putting facts about different things in the same table.

questions.question: A community centre keeps instructor phone numbers in every row of its CLASS_SESSION table. An instructor changes number, but only some rows get edited. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: An update anomaly: redundant copies were only partly changed, so the table now holds two different numbers for one instructor.

questions.question: The same centre cannot record a newly hired instructor until that instructor is assigned to a class, because instructor details live only in CLASS_SESSION. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: An insertion anomaly: you can't add one fact without also having an unrelated one.

questions.question: Deleting the last class an instructor taught also erases that instructor's phone number entirely. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: A deletion anomaly: removing one fact takes an unrelated fact down with it.

questions.question: A database system is an organization of five components. Match each to its role.

pairs.right: The physical devices the system runs on
The operating system, the DBMS, and application programs
Administrators, designers, programmers and end users
The rules and instructions governing how the system is used
The raw facts stored in the database itself

questions.explanation: Hardware, software, people, procedures and data — all five together make up the database system environment.

questions.question: Which DBMS function stores the definitions of data elements and their relationships?
questions.explanation: Data dictionary management. The data dictionary stores definitions of data elements and their relationships.

questions.question: Match each DBMS function to what it does.

pairs.right: Enforces user security and data privacy
Lets many users work concurrently without compromising integrity
Enables recovery of the database after a failure
Minimizes redundancy and maximizes consistency
Part of storage management; ensures efficient performance

questions.explanation: These are the standard DBMS functions. Notice that integrity management is defined in terms of redundancy and consistency.

questions.question: Which DBMS function makes it possible for many users to work in the database at once without corrupting it?
questions.explanation: Multiuser access control uses algorithms to ensure concurrent access without compromising integrity.

questions.question: In a query language, who decides HOW the result is produced?
options: The user, by writing the access path step by step
The system — the user specifies only what result they want
The application programmer, in the host language
questions.explanation: That's the defining property: users specify what they want, and the system determines how to produce it. This is why SQL is called nonprocedural.

questions.question: SQL stands for ______ Query Language.
questions.explanation: Structured Query Language — the de facto query language and data access standard, supported by nearly all DBMS vendors with slight variations.

questions.question: Every DBMS vendor implements SQL identically, so a query written for one product always runs unchanged on another.
questions.explanation: SQL is supported by nearly all vendors, but with slight variations — dialects differ, especially around dates and built-in functions.

questions.question: A simple representation of complex real-world data structures, useful for supporting a specific problem domain, is called a data ______.
questions.explanation: A data model. Data modeling is the act of creating one for a determined problem domain.

questions.question: Match each of the four basic building blocks of a data model to its definition.

pairs.right: A person, place, thing or event about which data is collected
A characteristic of an entity
An association among entities
A restriction placed on data to ensure integrity

questions.explanation: Entity, attribute, relationship, constraint — memorize these four; every ERD question is built out of them.

questions.question: When translating business rules into data model components, nouns generally become ______ and verbs generally become ______.
questions.explanation: Nouns translate into entities, verbs translate into relationships among entities.

questions.question: Relationships are always bidirectional — you have to read them from both ends.
questions.explanation: Because relationships run both ways, you ask two questions: how many B relate to one A, and how many A relate to one B.

questions.question: To determine the type of a relationship between entities A and B, you ask:
options: Only how many instances of B relate to one instance of A
How many instances of B relate to one A, AND how many instances of A relate to one B
Whether A or B was created first
questions.explanation: Both directions. Answering only one gives you half the cardinality and usually the wrong diagram.

questions.question: Match each relationship type to the two notations used for it.

pairs.right: M:N or *..*

questions.explanation: The colon form and the dotted UML-style form mean the same thing.

questions.question: Which naming convention is recommended for entity names?
options: Short codes that only the DBA needs to understand
Descriptive of the business environment, using terminology familiar to users
Always the plural of the attribute name
Sequential names such as TABLE1, TABLE2
questions.explanation: Good names are descriptive, match the business environment, and use terminology users already know — which promotes self-documentation.

questions.question: The relational model is based on the relation, which is another name for:
questions.explanation: A relation is a table or entity — a matrix of intersecting tuples (rows) and attributes (columns).

questions.question: Match each formal relational term to its everyday equivalent.

pairs.right: Table
Row
Column

questions.explanation: Relation/tuple/attribute is the formal vocabulary; table/row/column is what you'll actually say out loud.

questions.question: What does an RDBMS do that the raw relational model does not?
options: It eliminates the need for primary keys
It hides the complexities of the relational model from the user and makes it easier to implement
It removes the need for any data model at all
It converts the database into a file system
questions.explanation: An RDBMS performs the basic functions of earlier DBMS types while making the relational model easier to understand and implement, hiding its complexities.

questions.question: An entity ______, also called an entity occurrence, corresponds to a row in a relational table.
questions.explanation: Entity instance (or entity occurrence) = one row.

questions.question: ______ is the term used to label relationship types on an ERD (1:1, 1:M, M:N).
questions.explanation: Connectivity labels the relationship type. Cardinality expresses the specific numbers involved.

questions.question: Match each object-oriented term to its relational-model analogue.

pairs.right: Record
Entity or table
A property of an object

questions.explanation: An object is analogous to a record; a class is analogous to an entity/table — a class is a template from which individual objects are created.

questions.question: In the object-oriented data model, what distinguishes an object from a plain record?
options: An object contains data and relationships along with the operations to perform on that data
An object cannot be stored persistently
questions.explanation: The object holds data, relationships and its own operations together in a single structure.

questions.question: In an object-oriented class hierarchy, what does inheritance do?
options: Lets an object take on the methods and attributes of its parent classes
Copies every row from the parent table
Forces every class to have two parents
Removes attributes from the child class
questions.explanation: The hierarchy resembles an upside-down tree — each class has only one parent — and an object inherits the methods and attributes of its parent classes.

questions.question: In an object-oriented class hierarchy, each class may have many parent classes.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy resembles an upside-down tree in which each class has only one parent.

questions.question: Which pair correctly separates the logical model from the physical model?
options: Logical: what data is stored and how it relates. Physical: how it is actually implemented and stored
Logical: disk layout. Physical: business rules
Logical: only used after the database is built. Physical: only used in planning
They are two names for the same diagram
questions.explanation: Logical describes the structure as the user sees it; physical describes the actual implementation. The same distinction as logical vs physical format under data independence.

questions.question: Ordered from more abstract to less abstract, the levels of data modeling run:
options: Chen notation → Crow's Foot notation → DDL SQL
questions.explanation: Chen is the most abstract, Crow's Foot sits in the middle, and DDL SQL is the least abstract — it's the actual implementation.

questions.question: A data dictionary stores the definitions of data elements and their relationships.
questions.explanation: That's the definition given for the data dictionary, and data dictionary management is a core DBMS function.

questions.question: Which job title covers the design and implementation of conceptual, logical AND physical database environments?
questions.explanation: The Database Architect covers all three levels of the environment.
